review: You're thrown into an open world. You're given targets that you must kill, and in some instances, objectives to complete. That's it, the rest is up to you. You decide your weapon of choice to pull off the perfect hit; will it be the pistol? Shotgun? Assault Rifle? Submachine Gun? Sniper Rifle? You can spend the money that you earn from hits on different upgrades. Will you opt for a silencer on your pistol, or will you spend it on improved lockpicking skills? There are multiple different playstyles, and the choice is entirely up to you. Will you run in, guns blazing, killing anything that stands between you and your target? Or will you sneak in, using a disguise you stole from a guard that is now unconcious in the dumpster? How will you kill your targets? Will you poison their food? Strangle them? Snipe them? Rig a chandelier to fall on them? You choose how you play the game. You choose your definition of a perfect hit. First time players beware, however, you will find yourself spending lots of time doing trial-and-error to find the best ways to kill your target. If you enjoy games with linear gameplay where there's only one way to win, then you will probably not enjoy this game. However, if you want a sandbox stealth experience, where you get to decide how the game will play out, at $9.99, this game is perfect for you.

Hitman: Blood Money; the legend itself. I played this game as a kid and I still love it to this day.

To start off, I don't think Hitman is a stealth game more than it is a puzzle game. Every stage is its own open-ended puzzle that gives you multiple ways and tools to approach the situation any way you want.

It takes mechanics from older Hitmen, refines them and adds new ones. Gameplay has lots of details, such as peeking from keyholes, first person mode, concealing items, interacting with NPCs etc. Collecting guns from stages, and upgrading your weapons and items makes you feel you're constantly progressing and getting better. The stealth mechanics can feel a bit clunky today, but messing with disguises is still as fun as it was in 2006. The mechanics are also really easy to abuse and bug out, if you know how :P Still, getting a Silent Assassin rating, especially without any quicksaves is really satisfying.

Jesper Kyd's soundtrack is as amazing as it was in the previous Hitman games, I only wish Absolution and the new Hitman had his music :( It alone makes the game so much more immersive and gives every level life and energy.

Overall, Hitman: Blood Money still holds up really well today. Ignoring the tutorial mission, there isn't a single bad level in the game and they get constantly more complex along with your own progression. The amount of replay value it has makes it immortal for me.

When people talk Hitman there's usually one game they have in mind and that's Blood Money. Hitman is a series that boasted a novel concept which has somehow managed to remain pretty unique to this day (seriously - how many disguise-based stealth games are there?) and that gameplay evolved from game to game with Blood Money being the pinnacle (since Absolution went in a somewhat different direction closer to other stealth franchises like Splinter Cell).

Above all Blood Money is an action adventure game. Each mission provides quite a huge and open area with one ore more targets which need to be assassinated as well as the occasional non-assassination goal. Each map features many characters following basic routines and items or statics objects which can somehow be put to use. The beauty of Hitman lies in exploring the big and diverse environments, discovering usable objects, observing the targets and bystanders and then putting a brilliant plan together - and somewhat ironically the best and toughest plan is always the one where nobody dies, except for the targets of course. It gets even more complicated when you wish to make the deaths look like accidents and leave nothing behind (especially not that precious suit!). But even once you've developed that brilliant plan, there's still the matter of execution which requires perfect timing, with wits, patience and a good memory being the key to success - one mistake and everything goes to hell and there's not much left to do except mowing down everyone in your path.

As an action game Hitman is definitely sub-par but if you're up for it and are willing to spend ages on the same mission until you find and execute that perfect plan (or at least one perfect plan as often there's several ways to get that awesome Silent Assassin rating) there's nothing quite like it and a truly rewarding experience awaits you.

There's not much going on in terms of story, which is told through non-interactive cutscenes, but that doesn't keep the game from providing many very original locations and missions depicting the criminal underworld from a wide variety of angles, mostly ones you don't know from other games. To top it all off the action is accompanied by one of the greatest soundtracks to be ever heard in a video game, composed by legendary Jesper Kyd, providing a truly surreal atmosphere at times. What kind of graphics to expect everyone can clearly see on the screenshots.

Bottom line: if you are looking for an original stealth game or just want to know what all this Hitman talk is about - this is the game to go with.

Hitman Blood Money is an epitome of the Sandbox genre. This game requires skill and patience with almost endless possibilities to every mission. Not only are you allowed almost infinite options on how you come to face your target, but also how you chose to eliminate them.

Blood Money also offers an enjoyable experience to Stealth fans, but with a different approach. A majority of stealth games pride themselves on wall-to-wall, shadow-to-shadow gameplay; and while this can be very enjoyable and exciting; there are different ways to enjoy a stealth style experience; Blood Money is one of them! You are keeping your true identity hidden, not letting the enemy guards notice that their perimeter is breached; not allowing anyone to know you are even there. And when it all goes belly-up it still offers just as an enjoyable time trying to dig your-self out of that mess!

Obviously Blood Money has a few dated features like glitchy ragdolls; dated textures and filtering. But when you look past this, you see a game that far surpasses most modern day games in areas specifically such as the plot and level design. But if you are a gamer who when searching for new games mainly looks at the visual side of things, this may not be for you.

Blood Money also offers the ability for players to customize certain weapons with features such as silencers, scopes; different ammo types etc. Sadly, not all weapons found throughout the game allow you to do so, but this feature is still only found in very few games; including those of the current high budget new-releases. 

If I were playing this game at the time it was first released, it would have been a game with no noticeable flaws, but certain dated features cannot be ignored by today’s standards. Although the game’s base design is still without a doubt, impeccable, as are its plots and levels.

Booted up Hitman: Blood Money two days ago, after having not played it since 2006 or 2007.

Just beat it today.

Few things I found interesting about it:

- It's a 2006 multiplat release, which was during a generation where the vast majority of PC releases of console-centric games would often be *worse* than the console versions. With this title, you can run it at 4k just by making an ini edit, and it's flawless (doesn't break the UI or anything).

- As far as tech issues go, there was a bit of stuttering I fixed by going into the launcher and enabling both of the SLI settings (even though I'm not on SLI), but after that, game ran like it was made for my system. Then a lot of newer games have all these compatability issues and such until they're patched... were the people who made this game just better at what they did? Or have engines become so massive and unwieldy that it's more likely that things are going to fail than work? Or a combination of both?

- I had no bugs whatsoever.

- It has a first-person and third-person view - I know games did it before Blood Money (Morrowind for example), but I still think it's weird how a game from 2006 had this feature, and then it was a "big deal" when the GTAV re-release introduced a first-person mode.

- obviously the textures and lighting are a bit dated, but the game still looks great. I think it's almost the perfect balance between the awkward 3D years where I couldn't believe any of it was real because it was too ugly, and nowadays where everything that goes for this style is hyper-realistic and immersion breaking because of it. This game is actually better looking to me than a lot of modern games that have that hyper-realistic plastic-surgeon-with-OCD look.

- the music is still phenomenal, of course

- the game doesn't pester you or tell you explicitly how to do everything. There are a lot of hints on the lower difficulties (on the map), but if you want to play it as a proper stealth game, you have to figure out how all the pieces fit together on their own. It has a lot of space. The game is challenging in its own way, but due to the way it's all set up, it's actually relaxing to play. I'm not being yelled at or expected to be somewhere constantly or being given game information nonstop because the people who made it were afraid that if the game stopped talking to the player for 10 seconds I would shut it off and leave. I can just enjoy it without being nagged and feeling rushed along because of the "look here, do this, look here, shoot this" mentality. It lets you play.

- the worst thing about it is some character model pop-in, like the game runs a lower-poly version of them in the distance and when you get close makes them proper (I don't think I would've noticed this during my PS2 playthrough when it was new, but on PC at high-res and everything cranked it's pretty obvious)

- To boot every level is its own theme. If any copy-paste is going on it's minimal. There's more variety in the levels in a five hour game than I even saw in DOOM. Blood Money is genuinely interesting to play and anyone who hasn't played it yet needs to get it over with and understand why most people rant about most games. Once you have the best of everything, there's just a bunch of s*** you wade through hoping to find another game like Blood Money.

- Probably the best thing about it - it doesn't overstay its welcome. I played it on Expert (hadn't played in a loooong time so why would I Pro?), and beat every level with a Ghost, Professional or Silent Assassin rating, in just over 5 hours. I did remember some of the levels, but for the most part, I was blind here. It's refreshing, because they could've gone longer, they could've recycled assets to stretch it out, but why? Why do games need to last "forever"?

I did reinstall Absolution out of curiosity.  I ran it at max settings except for FXAA (which only blurs the image).  Even though the tech Absolution uses is way better, and the textures are obviously much higher res, the game isn't as nice to look at as Blood Money. 

Tech isn't everything. But when you don't know how to make a good game (something that I think needs to be a natural talent, like writing a good song or a good script - a few people have it, most people don't), you can at least learn how to push tech.  And I think those are the majority of people making games these days, which is why going back to Blood Money is... holy shit... most games really *are* as bad as I think they are.

But Blood Money is a masterpiece.

Two caveats to all this praise that some people may find impossibly bothersome:

- the FoV cannot be changed through official methods, I had no issue with it as-is, but there are third-party methods that may or may not work for you if you feel the only officially supported FoV is not acceptable.

- there is no cloud save support

June 27, 2018 edit: Booted it up with my 144hz display.  Instantly did 144fps no problem.  Sounds like that should be a no brainer, but a lot of games still cap at 60fps and break when decapped to go higher (for example, the PC version of Street Fighter IV), if they can be decapped at all.  This game had an awful lot of talent thrown at it.

Hitman: Blood Money is easily the best game in the series. And can easily be considered one of the greatest stealth games ever devised.

The reasons are numerous. Hitman Blood Money is a radical improvement over all of the previous games in the series. Taking elements that worked well from each of the previous games, and putting them in a single package. Coupled with numerous additions. Hits can now be completed by making the act resemble an accident, which typically is required to achieve a Silent Assassin rating. Additionally, after each hit you can view a newspaper which documents in detail what you did during the mission and even includes an artists rendering if you were seen by a witness. 

But that wasn't all. Hitman Blood Money was ahead of it's time in a lot of regards. Much like the previous games you could practice your weapons in 47's hideout. Along with collecting weapons in missions that you could use in other ones. But you could also upgrade your weapons with things like different stocks, magazines and silencers. Normal today but relatively unheard of at the time outside of uber tactical games. 

One flaw the previous Hitman games would occasionally have is missions would get a little samey after a while. They'd occasionally blend in together with a similar theme. Almost every mission in Hitman Blood Money is distinct, from an opera house hit to a mission taking place on a mississipi river boat. I remembered every single one, and their uniqueness adds a huge amount to how superior this game feels over the previous entries in the series. It really feels special and like the developers worked extremely hard on every single mission. 

It is just the quintessential Hitman game, technically flawless and masterfully polished. If every series had its own "Blood Money", we wouldn't need sequels.

Christ, I can be fangirling over this game for hours. It is such a gem; I first played it when I wasn't even a teen, so I was stupid, unattentive and horribly impatient. I didn't have the brainpower required to think of multiple strategies and ingenious ways to quietly assassinate target(s) and went on pretty much every assignment with guns blazing, which resulted in this cheap, primal, fleeting kind of fun – [i]haha, pistol go bang-bang, clink-clonk...[/i]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2507091803
While this can be moderately satisfying at times, especially after a dozen of unsuccessful attempts at being a world-class silent assassin, it all gets stale very quickly since this kind of playstyle is not where Blood Money really shines. Each mission is like a puzzle that you need to put together; I sometimes spent hours just wandering around and analysing various possibilities, studying the environment, watching people mingle and trying to memorise where they go and when, looking at the targets from afar and quietly following them wherever they lead me. Nothing makes sense for a while until it suddenly [i]clicks[/i], and you know what you will do and how exactly it will all go down. This is especially true about the levels towards the end – each one gets progressively more sprawling, with more complex layouts, as you approach the famous explosive finale. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2512878669
That is not to say that this is a flawless game; AI is often bugged and can be both omniscient or totally blind, depending on... whatever. The rating system, while no doubt a great addition that extends the playtime and entertainment value in this smart, unobtrusive kind of way, sometimes slaps a witness or two where there were none, or says that you were violent even though you were as humane as possible – "humane" in Blood Money means "strangling people with fibre wire" or "injecting poison into their bloodstream", but let us not delve too deep into ethics. All this means is that you can say goodbye to the coveted "Silent Assassin" rating. Guards see through walls, bodies put in bags suddenly get so stretched they occupy the entire room, women are passionately kissing with non-existent lovers, guys whom you don't intend to kill just die for no reason, dogs... [i]dogs can be witnesses[/i] – the whole enchilada. But I still love it. It's impossible to be seriously mad at this game – it gives you the finger and says that your playthrough sucked for no real reason, but you just sigh and restart obediently, grateful for a good enough excuse to replay that mission... [i]again.[/i]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2502887313
I will definitely take a look at the first three Hitman games in the near future, seeing that I have never played them before. This is how good Blood Money is – it will make you want to discover the series' roots, how this masterpiece came to be, what preceded it, what inspired the people behind it. 
* * *
The exciting dystopian world where cloning is a weapon of mass destruction. Agent 47's brutal ruthlessness and complete disregard for the lives of innocent people, animals or even partners. His morbid obsession with money. Sombre soundtrack. Beautiful, well-written and brilliantly executed cutscenes that feel like short films. Complete liberty in how you approach a task; enigmatic assignments, no handholding, no detailed explanations, no mercy. Diana's sexy Southern British accent. 
I need a lot more of this stuff... and then some.

If you turn down the difficulty settings, it is also really fun to just ignore stealth and kill everyone (including civilians).

I've been playing the Hitman series in order, and Blood Money is easily the best one of the four I've played so far. It improves on its predecessors in every conceivable way, and gives you a huge array of options for completing your missions.

Hitman 2 and 3 were pretty lenient on running and gunning tactics. Granted, I played those games on "Normal" difficulty, which gives you more saves and health, whereas I played Blood Money on "Expert", which gives you less health and saves, but even beyond difficulty level minutae, there are several systems in place to make sure 47 stays in line. Weapons are also no longer laser-precise, which means the tactic of "pull out the silenced pistol and pop your target in the head when no one's looking" isn't quite as reliable as before. If you miss your shot, you need to be ready to deal with it. There's also a "notoriety" system in play, where your actions in one level can raise the suspicion level in the next one if you don't take certain precautions (although it is trivially easy to bribe your notoriety down between levels). Things like closed circuit TV's also factor in, and you can steal the footage if you feel so inclined. Environmental options and "accidents"  also increase your capacity to go unseen. Nonlethal options are also improved, as 47 can now disarm people from the front (one time I blew my cover and ran around disarming everyone, which was hilarious), and new weapons such as the taser (which is hilarious to run around and hit people with) give you options to neutralize annoyances. You can also just punch someone unconscious, which raises a bit of a fuss, so use it sparingly. 

I appreciated that guards are a lot more "sensible" in the sense that they won't automatically jump down your throat for a slight infraction. Walking into an area you aren't allowed in doesn't instantly cause people to gun you down, but rather they will tell you to leave and escort you out, which feels much more realistic.

Visually, the game looks great. It looks much better than most other games from 2006, and still looks very clean and snazzy today. Certain levels, such as the Mardi Gras level and a Heaven/Hell themed rave feature incredibly dense crowds that would be impressive in one of today's game, but are mindblowing to see in a game that's more than 10 years old. I was actually surprised to find out there exists a version of this for Playstation 2, because the game just seems so "next gen", as it were. Great lighting adds to the game's sense of atmosphere, as does yet another fantastic soundtrack by Jesper Kyd.

FInally, there's actually a really good story going, which has several interesting threads that weave in and out of each mission. One thing I really liked is that you get a newspaper after each level that not only describes your performance in the form of a news article, but fills you in on other goings-on in the world, many of which gradually become important to the main plotline. Just be sure not to try and screenshot the newspapers, this crashes the game! I feel like the first three Hitman games were pretty weak in the story department, so finally having a spy story with some actual intrigue was a refreshing and enjoyable change.

Overall, Blood Money is the Hitman franchise finally hitting it's pace. Everything is meticulously designed to be a smooth, excellent stealth game. Fans of the series or stealth games in general would do well to pick this one up.

[h1]There is a Reason Good Game Design Doesn't Get Old[/h1]

Hitman Blood Money is one of the greatest examples of why good game design is timeless. The game has amazing level variety. Each level has so much soul, and as you're learning each of them, you feel like the devs are watching you as you play through them. Meticulous level and sandbox design really is what IOI did best, and it shows.

One of the special things Blood Money did even better than the other games is the notoriety system. It's not a huge part of the game, but it adds a meaningful layer that makes it worth going for higher ratings. I love it when games actually make going for higher ratings a core part of the experience. Depending on how you play, the way NPCs react to you changes drastically, even though it's relatively easy to get around the notoriety system by simply paying the required amount of money. Nevertheless, I just love it because the game actually acknowledges the fact that it does matter how good of a ranking you get in a mission, and the overall progression feels more personal.

Overall, Blood Money is an incredible stealth sandbox with great humor, a relatively good story, and a lot of soul, something that is not very easily explained but only truly felt when playing and mastering the game.

Classic Hitman! There's a reason people say this is the best Hitman game so far, and I totally agree.
I used to play this game in my early teens, and bought it again so I could have it on Steam (yeah, it is THAT good).


The missions are well thought-out, and take place on very unique locations. Each level is completely different from the other, and you never get the "I think I've done this before" feeling, because this game completely ditches the "Just go there and kill that guy" mechanic. The methods you choose to kill your target (or targets) really do feel unique, and the same thing will never work twice. You have to analyze your surroundings, the relationship between your targets and think about what will happen if you do X (this is one of the few games I ever played where the mission briefing REALLY is worth reading, because it gives you very important insight on the targets).


If you're not a fan of changing disguises and just want to put your foot on the door and shoot everybody, you can also do that. This games has one of the most diverse arsenals I've ever seen, second only to the GTA series. There's a lot of guns to collect from each level, and you can also customize 47's personal guns with silencers, ammo types, barrels, sights, etc... 


The game also features a notoriety system. If you made a lot of noise on the last level, was caught on camera, or left a lot of witnesses behind, people will go to the police and report what you look like, so, in the next level you play, people are going to recognize you (this totally blew my mind at the time). But, if you plan on going full Rambo, don't worry. You can also pay (with in-game money, obviously. Looking at you, EA....) to lower your notoriety so you don't have as much of a hard time on the next level.


The replay-value is great, too; there's just so many ways to complete each level, that you can definitely play the same mission countless times and still find some hidden interaction or an alternate way to do the mission.

First off, if you're thinking of playing this game, DO NOT PLAY IT EXPECTING A MODERN GAME. Its a product of its time with a lot of aged mechanics. Its a very old school game. If you like the idea but don't like old aged games, go play HITMAN 2, which carries all the good of this game but with the touch of modernity.

But about the game itself, its a very good trial and error stealth game. Getting you to investigate the whole site and surroundings and think to yourself "How can I kill this person ?". You will die a lot, but thats the magic of the game. Figuring out what you can and can't do. What can you get away with and can't. At its core, its a puzzle game about assassination. You're given the tools and the world and just told "Figure it out". No clues, no helping hand. You just study and figure everything out by yourself. It feels very rewarding when you kill a target, finally when all the pieces fit together and you get to kill them.

The AI is very abuseable. You can distract then by throwing anything in your inventory and just get them from behind. Distract them and lockpick a door. Or get them to take your weapons to the security room so you can get them later. There's a huge window of things you can do and things you can abuse.

Its a very niche game, and if you're not into stealth or puzzle games, you won't enjoy it. But if you are, this would be a really fun time for you.

To use custom resolutions (especially for 16:9 widescreens, like 1080p):

1) Find Hitman: Blood Money in your library.
2) Right click to the game.
3) Click on Properties, then Local Files, then Browse.
4) You'll see HitmanBloodMoney.ini in game files, right click on it and select Edit.
5) You'll see a text like Resolution 800x600, change it according to your resolution like Resolution 1920x1080.
6) Run the game and enjoy it.

Also, limited saves are per episode not the whole game.

Good luck!

If you just played the new Hitman games and wondering if you're going to play the older ones, Hitman: Blood Money is a great place to start. The graphics may seem a bit aged, but in my opinion it still holds up. Some maps are really cool, even more interesting than the newer titles. I should mention there are almost no one that can see through your disguise, with the exception of targets and if they discover the body of the disguised person. Of course, strategy is still required to find the best ways to dispose of your targets, preferrably quietly.

For first-time players, the levels could be confusing, as opportunities to kill the targets are not shown directly. The easiest way is to wait until the targets are alone, and kill them, though doing this everytime kinda takes the fun out of it. If you're looking into the Hitman franchise, get the Essential Collection bundle, since it contains the newer Hitman games and some stable, older ones, even though it doesn't have the (sadly unstable) original games.

This game is a master-class in level design, implementing the philosophy of letting the player choose their approach and play-style to near perfection. This game's replayability value is outstanding. However, for any first-time players, even those who are experienced with other Hitman titles, Blood Money definitely takes getting used to.

Menu navigation is likely the biggest headache you'll encounter, at least initially. For example, when there are multiple bodies, guns and a door nearby, you can't bind WASD to navigate that "use" menu, as it will make Agent 47 move away from what you're interacting with. Instead, make sure to use your mouse's scroll-wheel, but if that doesn't work, the best alternative is to bind menu up and down to your keyboard's traditional direction keys.

The game has aged remarkably well, but if you have a high-refresh rate gaming monitor running over 60 frames a second, this will cause rare, obscure issues like not being able to fire your weapons in the slow-motion death scenes. Very high resolutions like 4K and over are also not natively supported, so a mod or an edit to the configuration files will be needed.

Aside from these nuisances, this game is so much fun that it's worth putting up with its technical hiccups. The first-person mode is a blast, and a highly welcome option in many scenarios. There are a lot of missions to play through, and each of them is so well planned, that there can be dozens of different ways to complete a mission well.

The available four difficulty settings scale intuitively, and the AI is more than serviceable. The four default weapons can be upgraded rather extensively, and this is one of the few games I know of where you can put a suppressor on a shotgun! Aside from those four defaults, there's a heap of special weapons to collect throughout all the missions, even a humble air rifle.

Amusingly, this game is very clearly designed for a subtle, stealthy approach to gameplay, yet you are given a wide assortment of destructive weapons, for those special times when you feel like throwing stealth to the wind.

"What do you want in this mission? No weapons at all for maximum sneakiness, or a double-drum magazine on your M4 assault rifle loaded with armor-piercing bullets? Can complete this mission with only your fiber-wire, or do you think waltzing into the target's office with a magazine-fed short-barrel SPAS-12 is more appropriate?"

A personal favoured title, and one I'll repeatedly return to over the years. Very highly recommended!

To start off, this game is awesome, and surprisingly good considering its age. I've never played a Hitman game before this one, it was cheap and had higher reviews than the other older games in the series, and I would now definitely consider myself a fan of the series.

This game is a "social stealth" game, meaning that you hide in plain sight, utilizing disguises, subterfuge, and clever tricks of your environment to take down your targets, and walk away nonchalantly from either the chaos (if you like a more comedic high profile approach), everyone's lack of awareness that any killing happened at all (if you want to be a ninja), or from everyone's shock that a chandelier "accidentally" fell on the party host's face RIGHT when his wife blew up from a faulty BBQ propane tank (the best, most difficult, and rewarding way to do things).

I guess you COULD just run in guns blazing, but you would get a lot of points deducted, it'd kill the fun of the game, and honestly I think it'd be the most difficult approach. Besides, you wouldn't get the pleasure of sneaking into a party dressed as a clown and have your target's slutty alcoholic wife try to bang you. This game has amazing humor.

Honestly, the best way to describe this game would be to look at it as a stealth puzzle game. You have a load of options, environmental hazards, paths through the level, disguises, and killing techniques, some work great, some need some ingenuity. All in all, it's up to you to figure out the level and how you want to do things, whatever methods you discover work best, or are the most entertaining. 

There were some problems, however, both with the gameplay and with compatibility/running the game, which would be dishonest not to address. For one, the controls are ported from the console's controller, it seems, so you have a lot of commands needlessly sharing the same button, which did lead to some mission failures (having the "open door" and "take out explosives hidden in suitcase right in front of guards" commands sharing the same button is infuriating for obvious reasons). The other big problem I had was the final, FINAL short bonus stage during the credits being an absolutely maddening firefight, where I had to listen to the first minute of the same song everytime I failed.

So for tech and compatibility issues, there are quite a few. Sometimes after a mission, when the newspaper headline pops up, it crashes your game before it saves. My god. The fix for this is to open the game in the settings launcher, change shader quality to "High - shader model 2", and change the "SLI" settings so both "Override SLI" and "Enable SLI" options are checked off. At least it solved the problem for me. Also, sometimes the game won't close right, and Steam will think it's still running when it's not (hence the 33 or 34 hours on record. My friends probably thought it was strange that I played this game for 10 hour sessions at a time), so you'll have to legit restart your computer in order for Steam to be able to re-open it. ALSO (yeah, I know it's a long caveat list) sometimes my CPU would be at 100%, and that was from "rundll32.exe" being messed with and running in the background. Just end that process in Task Manager on Windows, and you'll be fine.

So I know it can be annoying, but it says a lot about how much I enjoyed this game that all that troubleshooting didn't ruin my experience of this game. But, obviously, if you're the type who that sort of thing ruins the game for you, I guess just skip this one, but you'd be missing out.

All in all, this game is $10 full price (worth it), and $2 on sale (an absolute steal). Another plus is that this game can probably run on a potato laptop, although I did not test this theory on my potato laptop. I know not everyone has a desktop setup, if not, this is a game you'd want in your limited library. I look forward to playing through the newest 2 Hitman games.

Hitman: Blood Money was and still is quite the changeup compared to the all-time glorious Hitman: Contracts, its direct predecessor. While it really opened up the game mechanics by adding hundreds of bystanders and civilians to many of the levels, which also happen to be some of the best designed levels and environments of the entire franchise, Blood Money also butchered backstory continuity between levels and added a very annoyingly rudimentary unlock system which gave you access to many weapons and gadgets you would end up never even using once if you wanted to get a Silent Assassin rating, making most of these items entirely obsolete and therefore soiling the entire unlocking process.

Those little flaws aside, Blood Money managed to heavily build upon the best elements of the Hitman series, meaning it featured even more ridiculous accident kills, some levels with vertical gameplay (the Casino and Opera being two of my favourites) and even more different viable approaches than were already introduced in Hitman: Contracts.

And while Blood Money is currently eleven years old, it aged really well, plays even better than Absolution and can still be enjoyed to its full extent without any drawbacks. This should not be missing from any person's library with a love for stealth games and is more than worth its asking price. On sale this should be an automatic purchase.
